doc: OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions. The dialect every other rule file may import: it is what a framework emits when it emits nothing of its own.

carriers.doc: The model's own output. One emission, so two tool calls in it are two calls whether or not the provider sent ids - a model asking twice looks exactly like this.
The completion, under the older convention name. Same fact, older spelling.
What this span produced, as an event. On a generation span this is the model's own emission.
A span's own record of a tool it ran: one emission it produced.

One emission too, but received: the framework handing a past result back to a model. Its time is the hand-back, and it is input to whatever the span then produces. Reading it as output made a re-sent result look like a generation's own answer.
A re-sent turn: history by definition.
A system turn inside the conversation stream. Deliberately not a detached request frame: an event in a stream is in-band and may be a turn, framed by its position.
The awkward one: a replay for most frameworks, and the actual output for a choiceless generation span. Read as a snapshot here; direction is decided downstream.

On a model call, the per-message events are the request, one event per message in the order the request lists them, so they are one array and carry an ordering family. The order is the only evidence that places a block a request introduces: Strands for TypeScript omits reasoning from a turn's reported output, so a later request's history is where it first appears, and time cannot place it, because OpenTelemetry JavaScript lets spans' clocks disagree by up to a millisecond. Declaring the family was tried once before and reverted because it repaired nothing; on `strands-js/multi_turn` it places that reasoning before the next question in both telemetry modes, and it moves no other fixture.
An earlier turn's reply inside a model call's request: a member of the request's ordered array, like `semconv.event.user_message.request`.
The prompt, under the older convention name.
The conversation as this span received it, as an event.
What this span produced, in one payload. Ordered, its own, and two of anything in it are two - the attribute form of gen_ai.choice. Being an emission is what keeps a response's parts together.
The family's root: the array itself, which expands into one observation per message. A key *beneath* it is one message's own member and stays whole.
What this span received: a conversation as it saw it, which may re-state earlier turns.
The family's root: the array itself, which expands into one observation per message. A key *beneath* it is one message's own member and stays whole.

The system prompt a model was given, reported beside the conversation rather than inside it. A detached request frame: it asserts 'this precedes every other input of the request that carried me', which is a constraint rather than a position.
A tool span's own result under the current conventions. One emission - a tool is called once.
The arguments that tool span was handed: the same pair, differing only in direction. The clearest case for direction being its own fact rather than something inferred from shape.
The deprecated indexed request family. Received, like the current spelling.
The deprecated indexed response family.
Anything else under the current request namespace: received by definition.
Anything else under the current response namespace: produced by definition.

messages.doc: The request as an indexed attribute family - `gen_ai.prompt.0.role`, `.0.content`, `.1.role`. A list of objects flattened into dotted keys because OTel attributes are a flat map. `content` is required because an index exists as soon as any key mentions it, and the family also holds keys that are not turns.
The response in the same encoding.
The system prompt as a parts array. Wrapped with the parts under `parts` rather than `content`, which is how the conventions write a structured instruction.
The request, stored as it arrived: normalisation happens at query time, so the payload is kept whole.
The response, stored as it arrived.

A whole conversation reported on an agent-run span. Kept as its literal message array so query-time expansion produces the individual user, assistant, and tool turns; the snapshot carrier semantics then deduplicate those turns against model-call spans.

A tool call. Built as a `tool_use` block, not a bare object under a role: the block shape is what carries the name and the id through normalisation, and the id is what lets the result be paired with this call rather than guessed at by content. The name falls back to the span name because the conventions prescribe `execute_tool {name}` there, and it defaults to empty rather than being omitted - a block whose shape requires a name carries an empty one, and the two are different values to anything hashing the payload.
The answer to it, as a `tool_result` block carrying the same id. Here the name is *omitted* when absent rather than defaulted, which is what the extractor did - the block is identified by its id.
The convention's own tool schemas, as one JSON array.
A list of tool *names* an agent had available - which tools, not what they take.

The convention's inference-details event is a *container*: its own attributes are the request and the response, so the container itself is not a message - reporting it as well would give the conversation twice. Read on a tool span too: the retired extractor answered this event before any tool-span check.
The response side of the same container. Read on a tool span too: the retired extractor answered this event before any tool-span check.

The convention's own single-tool triple: a name, its documentation and its schema, as three attributes. Emitted only where the name is one a caller could use - one dialect reports a synthetic aggregate under a name in parentheses, which is not a tool. Ranked last among the tool readers, which is where the retired block sat: it ran after every other definition had been collected, and merging keeps the *first* of two equal-quality definitions with one name - so the order decides which description and schema win, not merely the stored bytes.

all.doc: A synthetic aggregate is reported under a parenthesised name; a tool anyone can call begins like an identifier.

span_facts.doc: The convention's own statement, and the pair of attributes that only appear together on a call being run.

signals.doc: The operation the span reports performing.
A tool name *and* a call id. The name alone sits on a model span that merely mentions a tool; with an id it is a call being run.

message_events.name: gen_ai.system.message
message_events.doc: A system instruction, as an event.

message_events.name: gen_ai.assistant.message
message_events.doc: An assistant turn - a replay for most dialects, and the reply itself for a choiceless generation span.

message_events.name: gen_ai.choice
message_events.doc: What the model chose: this span's own output.

message_events.name: gen_ai.content.prompt
message_events.doc: The deprecated spelling of the request.

message_events.name: gen_ai.content.completion
message_events.doc: The deprecated spelling of the response.

message_events.name: gen_ai.tool.message
message_events.doc: A tool result handed back to a model.

message_events.name: gen_ai.client.inference.operation.details
message_events.doc: A container whose own attributes are the request and the response.

log_events.name: gen_ai.system.message
log_events.doc: A system instruction, as a log record whose body members are the event's attributes.

log_events.name: gen_ai.user.message
log_events.doc: A user turn, as a log record whose body members are the event's attributes - the shape the OpenTelemetry OpenAI and botocore instrumentations emit by default.

log_events.name: gen_ai.assistant.message
log_events.doc: An assistant turn, as a log record whose body members are the event's attributes.

log_events.name: gen_ai.tool.message
log_events.doc: A tool result handed back to a model, as a log record whose body members are the event's attributes.

log_events.name: gen_ai.choice
log_events.doc: What the model chose, as a log record whose body carries `index`, `finish_reason` and `message`.

log_events.name: gen_ai.client.inference.operation.details
log_events.doc: The inference-details container as a log record: its own attributes are the request and the response, read by the same container readings as the span event.

event_roles.name: gen_ai.content.prompt
event_roles.doc: The deprecated spelling of the request, which is a user turn.

event_roles.name: gen_ai.tool.message
event_roles.doc: A tool message means opposite things by span: on a chat span it is what the tool returned, and on a tool execution span it is the arguments the assistant passed. The tool-span reading is `assistant` rather than a role of its own so it cannot merge with the tool's *output* during correlation - `tool_call` maps to assistant anyway, so it is the same statement.

event_roles.name: gen_ai.tool.result
event_roles.doc: A name a rule assigns with `tag_as`, not one a producer emits: a bundled result set, whose members are the tool's answers whatever span carries them.

event_roles.name: gen_ai.assistant.message
event_roles.doc: Always the assistant, on either kind of span - it is a re-sent turn for most dialects and the reply itself for a choiceless generation span, and neither is a tool's output.

event_roles.name: gen_ai.choice
event_roles.doc: What the model chose on a chat span, and on a tool execution span what the *tool* returned - the span's own output either way, which is why the role follows the span.

event_roles.name: gen_ai.content.completion
event_roles.doc: The deprecated spelling of the response, following `gen_ai.choice` exactly.

content_blocks.doc: The conventions' binary part: base64 `content`, with an optional `mime_type`. An earlier draft put the payload under `data`, which the provider formats read; this spelling fell through to an unknown block, so an image or a document a user sent rendered as raw JSON. Logfire's Anthropic instrumentation omits the MIME type, so the bytes name it. AgentScope spells the type `media_type`, which is read too.

The conventions' reference part: a `uri` with an optional `mime_type`. Logfire writes an inline image this way, as a `data:` URI, so it was kept as an unknown block; the media type comes from the declaration, the URI, or the bytes.
